# Refractive errors

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Ophthalmology > Retina and vision > Refractive errors*

[Original Article Link](/library/vF0AP3)

---

## Summary

Refractive errors (ametropia) are conditions in which light rays entering the <u>eye</u> are not focused on the <u>retina</u>, leading to blurred <u>vision</u>. Abnormalities in <u>eye anatomy</u> affecting the <u>refractory media</u> (e.g., axial <u>eye</u> length, corneal curvature) lead to <u>myopia</u>, <u>hyperopia</u>, <u>astigmatism</u>, and/or <u>presbyopia</u>. <u>Visual acuity testing</u> is used to detect refractive errors; diagnosis and severity are determined by <u>refraction</u> testing as part of a <u>comprehensive eye examination</u>. Treatment typically involves corrective lenses (glasses, contact lenses) or <u>refractive surgery</u>. Individuals with refractive errors, particularly those with a high <u>myopic</u> error, are at increased risk for other <u>eye</u> conditions (e.g., <u>retinal detachment</u>, <u>glaucoma</u>, <u>cataracts</u>). Routine <u>visual acuity testing</u> is recommended for children and <u>adolescents</u>; <u>screening recommendations</u> for adults vary.

---

## Definitions

### Emmetropia




* A physiologic state of <u>vision</u> in which rays of light entering the relaxed <u>eye</u> are focused on the <u>retina</u>

* Results in clear <u>vision</u>





### Myopia [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




* A refractive error in which light rays entering the <u>eye</u> are focused <u>anterior</u> to the <u>retina</u>

* Increased axial length of the <u>eye</u> or, less commonly, increased <u>refraction</u> → <u>focal point</u> <u>anterior</u> to the <u>retina</u>

* Nearby objects appear in focus, while objects in the distance appear blurry.





![Emmetropia, myopia, and hyperopia](media/d2b7dcxhmk16ydr5bhvla8ur.jpg)

Emmetropia, myopia, and hyperopia




### Hyperopia [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




* A refractive error in which light rays entering the <u>eye</u> are focused <u>posterior</u> to the <u>retina</u>

* Decreased axial length of the <u>eye</u> → <u>focal point</u> <u>posterior</u> to the <u>retina</u>

* Nearby objects appear blurry, while objects in the distance appear in focus.





![Emmetropia, myopia, and hyperopia](media/d2b7dcxhmk16ydr5bhvla8ur.jpg)

Emmetropia, myopia, and hyperopia




### Presbyopia [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




* An age-related decrease in the power of <u>accommodation</u> of the <u>eye</u>

* ↓ <u>Lens</u> elasticity, ↓ strength of <u>ciliary muscle</u>, and ↓ <u>lens</u> curvature → ↓ <u>lens</u> <u>accommodation</u> (focusing on an object up close)

* Typically leads to the inability to focus on nearby objects.





![Presbyopia](media/k0k0d3xxmps2t18aqm2zb6ds.jpg)

Presbyopia




### Astigmatism [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




* A refractive error in which abnormal curvature of the <u>cornea</u> leads to two or more focal points, causing blurred <u>vision</u> at all distances

* Abnormal curvature of the <u>cornea</u> → distorted <u>refraction</u> → two or more focal points, which can be <u>anterior</u> and/or <u>posterior</u> to the <u>retina</u>, depending on the curvature





![Regular astigmatism](media/vdpong0ee3n4fwabg2yfok7d.jpg)

Regular astigmatism

## Overview

| <br>Overview of refractive errors [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0) |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  | Clinical features | Management | Complications |
| <u>Myopia</u> | <br><br>* Clear near <u>vision</u><br><br>* Blurred far <u>vision</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Glasses with <u>concave</u> (diverging) lenses<br><br>* Contact lenses<br><br>* <u>Orthokeratology</u><br><br>* <u>Refractive surgery</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Retinal detachment</u><br><br>* <u>Myopic</u> <u>macular degeneration</u><br><br>* <u>Glaucoma</u><br><br>* <u>Cataracts</u><br><br>* <u>Visual field</u> defects<br><br><br> |
| <u>Hyperopia</u> | <br><br>* Blurred near <u>vision</u><br><br>* Clear far <u>vision</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* Glasses with <u>convex</u> (converging) lenses<br><br>* Contact lenses<br><br>* <u>Refractive surgery</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Closed-angle glaucoma</u> [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)<br><br> |
| <u>Presbyopia</u> | <br>* Similar to <u>hyperopia</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Similar to <u>hyperopia</u><br><br>* Topical <u>pilocarpine</u><br><br><br> | <br>* None<br><br> |
| <u>Astigmatism</u> | <br>* Blurred <u>vision</u> at all distances<br><br> | <br><br>* Regular <u>astigmatism</u>: cylindrical lenses<br><br>* Irregular <u>astigmatism</u>: specialty contact lenses and/or <u>refractive surgery</u><br><br><br> | <br>* Early onset (< 5 years of age) increases the risk for <u>amblyopia</u>. [[2]](/library/Q3duRp0)<br><br> |





> [!TIP]
> Individuals with refractive errors who develop <u>cataracts</u> may experience a temporary improvement in <u>vision</u> (<u>second sight</u>) due to the change in the <u>refractive index</u> of the <u>lens</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Increased time spent outdoors, low-dose topical <u>atropine</u>, multifocal lenses, and <u>orthokeratology</u> can slow progression mild to moderate <u>myopia</u> in children and <u>adolescents</u>. [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




> [!WARNING]
> Individuals with high refractive errors (≥ 6 <u>diopters</u> of <u>myopia</u>, ≥ 3 <u>diopters</u> of <u>hyperopia</u>, or ≥ 3 <u>diopters</u> of regular <u>astigmatism</u>) are at increased risk for complications and other ocular conditions compared to individuals with less severe refractive errors. [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)

## Clinical features

* Blurred <u>vision</u>: See “<u>Overview of refractive errors</u>” for features specific to the type of refractive error.

* <u>Diplopia</u> [[3]](/library/S2dyS60)

* Asthenopia: symptoms associated with overuse of the eyes [[3]](/library/S2dyS60)

* <u>Eye pain</u>

* <u>Lacrimation</u>

* Burning or itching eyes

* Headache associated with refractive errors [[4]](/library/f2dkS60)

* Aggravated by visual tasks at distances at which <u>vision</u> is impaired and alleviated upon task cessation

* Chronic; usually daily

* Typically worse in the second half of the day

* Improves significantly after correction of refractive error(s)

---

## Corrective lenses

* Glasses and contact lenses help focus light rays entering the <u>eye</u> on the <u>retina</u>.

* Multifocal (e.g., bifocal, trifocal, or progressive) lenses correct <u>visual acuity</u> at multiple distances.

* The modality used is typically based on patient preference.





### Glasses [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




#### Indications




* First-line treatment for refractive errors

* Contraindications to contact lenses

* Need or desire for <u>eye</u> protection

* Contact <u>lens</u> wearers: to prevent overuse of contact lenses





#### Types




* <u>Convex</u>, <u>concave</u>, or cylindrical lenses are used depending on the type of refractive error.

* See “<u>Overview of refractive errors</u>” for specific details.





### Contact lenses [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




#### Indications




* Refractive error

* Need or desire to decrease use of glasses

* Inadequate <u>vision</u> improvement with glasses

* <u>Myopia</u> treated with <u>orthokeratology</u>

* <u>Keratoconus</u> [[6]](/library/tedX060)

* <u>Aphakia</u> [[7]](/library/Fedg060)





> [!TIP]
> Individuals who use contact lenses should also have a pair of glasses to prevent contact <u>lens</u> overuse. [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




#### <u>Relative contraindications</u>




* <u>Conjunctivitis</u> (e.g., <u>keratoconjunctivitis sicca</u>, blepharoconjunctivitis)

* Corneal exposure (e.g., due to incomplete <u>eyelid</u> closure)

* Corneal abnormalities (e.g., <u>keratitis</u>)

* <u>Ocular rosacea</u>

* Use of topical ophthalmologic <u>steroids</u>





#### Types




* Soft (e.g., soft hydrogel, silicone hydrogel) or rigid gas permeable

* Disposable (discarded daily, weekly, or monthly) or conventional lenses (replaced at least annually)





> [!TIP]
> Most lenses are worn while awake and removed for sleeping; extended-wear contact lenses can be worn continuously for up to 30 days. The <u>FDA</u> recommends removing extended-wear contact lenses at least once a week for cleaning and <u>disinfection</u>.




#### Contact lens hygiene




Counsel all patients on the following recommendations. [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)[[8]](/library/GD1BfQ0)




* Wash hands with soap and water before handling lenses.

* Do not wear contact lenses while sleeping unless prescribed (e.g., for <u>orthokeratology</u>).

* Avoid contact of lenses with water.

* Clean and store lenses with disinfecting contact <u>lens</u> solution; not water.

* Discard the used solution completely before refilling the storage case.

* Replace contact lenses and storage cases as directed.





> [!TIP]
> Risk of infection is reduced by using daily disposable contact lenses and increased if contact lenses are worn while sleeping (e.g., extended-wear lenses or daily lenses left in overnight). [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Acanthamoeba</u>, which causes <u>Acanthamoeba keratitis</u>, is commonly found in tap water and other water sources. Recommend removal of lenses before swimming or showering. [[1]](/library/3VdS8K0)




#### Complications




* Microbial <u>keratitis</u>

* <u>Corneal ulcer</u>, <u>neovascularization</u>, thinning

* <u>Giant papillary conjunctivitis</u>
